lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Get ready! What you will learn

pages.body:
> 🎯 **What you will learn in this chapter**
- How to sort materials into solids, liquids and gases
- Why liquids matter to human life and how to take care of them
- Why solids matter to human life and how to take care of them
- How the periodic table sorts elements into metals, nonmetals and noble gases

pages.title: What is matter
pages.body: Look around you. Your desk, the water you drink and the air you breathe are all made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Mass means it can be weighed. Matter is made of tiny particles. These particles are too small to see. The way the particles are packed and the way they move tell us if a material is a solid, a liquid or a gas. We call this the state of matter.

pages.title: The three states of matter
pages.body:
Look at the picture below. Each dot stands for a tiny particle of matter.

[[img:ifhotim80]]

| **Property** | **Solid** | **Liquid** | **Gas** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shape** | Has its own fixed shape | Takes the shape of its container | Fills up all the space in its container |
| **Volume** | Fixed volume | Fixed volume | No fixed volume |
| **How the particles are packed** | Packed close together in neat rows | Close together but not neat | Spread far apart |
| **How the particles move** | They just shake in one place (Vibrate) | They slide past each other | They move fast in every direction (Randomly) |
| **Can it be squeezed smaller (Compressibility)** | No | Only a little | Yes, very easily |
| **Examples** | Wood, stone, an iron nail, ice | Water, palm oil, kerosene | Air, oxygen, steam, carbon dioxide |

questions.q: Matter is best described as
o: Anything that has mass and takes up space
Something with no mass at all
questions.e: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, and every material around you, from the chair you sit on to the water you drink to the air you breathe, is a form of matter.

questions.q: A solid has
o: A fixed shape and a fixed volume
No fixed shape and no fixed volume
Only a fixed shape but no fixed volume
questions.e: A solid is a material that has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, meaning it does not change its shape or spread out to fill a container the way a liquid or gas would.

questions.q: A liquid has
o: A fixed shape but no fixed volume
A fixed volume but takes the shape of its container
Neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume
questions.e: A liquid is a material that has a fixed volume but no fixed shape, meaning it always takes on the shape of whatever container holds it, while the total amount of liquid stays the same.

questions.q: A gas has
o: A fixed shape and a fixed volume
Neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume
questions.e: A gas is a material that has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume, meaning it spreads out to completely fill whatever container it is placed in, however large that container may be.

questions.q: In a solid, the particles are
o: Packed closely together and only vibrate in place
Spread far apart and move freely
questions.e: The particles in a solid are packed closely together in a regular arrangement and can only vibrate in place, not move freely past one another, which is why a solid keeps its shape unless a force is applied to break, cut or reshape…

questions.q: In a gas, the particles are
o: Spread far apart and move freely in all directions
questions.e: The particles in a gas are spaced far apart and move freely and quickly in every direction, which is why a gas cannot be seen easily and will always expand to occupy all the available space.

questions.q: A liquid can be poured from one container into another mainly because its particles
o: Can slide and move past one another
questions.e: The particles in a liquid are still close together but can slide and move past one another, which is why a liquid can flow and be poured from one container into another.

questions.q: Name three ways a solid is different from a gas.

parts.a: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume, so it fills all the space in its container. The particles of a solid are packed close together and only vibrate, but the particles of a gas are far apart and move fast in every direction. A gas can be squeezed easily, a solid cannot.

ideas.t: A solid has a fixed shape, a gas does not
A solid has a fixed volume, a gas fills its container
Particles in a solid are packed close, in a gas they are far apart
Particles in a solid only vibrate, in a gas they move fast and freely
A gas can be squeezed (compressed), a solid cannot

questions.q: Cooking gas in your home is stored inside a strong metal cylinder with a tight cover. Explain why it cannot be stored in an open plastic bag instead.

parts.a: Cooking gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume, so it would spread out and escape from an open plastic bag. It is stored as a liquid under pressure, so it needs a strong metal cylinder with a tight cover.

ideas.t: A gas spreads out and would escape from an open bag
The cylinder is strong and tight to hold the gas under pressure

pages.title: Sorting materials from your surroundings
pages.body:
You can look at everyday materials and sort them by state. Some materials may surprise you.

- Toothpaste and honey act like very thick liquids.
- Butter is a solid at room temperature. It melts and becomes a liquid when it is heated.
- Cooking gas is stored as a liquid inside the cylinder under pressure. As soon as it is released, it turns into gas.

These examples show us that the state of a material can change. Heat and pressure can change a material from one state to another.

> 🧪 **Activity 1** Work in a group. Collect eight to ten materials from your school compound or home. Examples are a stone, water, cooking oil, air in a balloon, chalk, an exercise book, palm wine and a nail. Draw a table with these headings. Material, Texture, Appearance, Colour, Shape, State. Fill in the table for each material. Talk about your answers as a class. Explain why you placed each material under its state.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a solid?
questions.e: Solids include your school desk, a pencil, and a stone in the schoolyard.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a liquid?
questions.e: Water, cooking oil, and fruit juice are all examples of liquids.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a gas?
questions.e: Gases include the air inside a football, the steam rising from hot food, and the smoke from a cooking fire, since steam and smoke, though sometimes visible as clouds of tiny droplets or particles, behave like gases in the way they…

parts.a: Solids: wood (for building and furniture) and stone (for foundations and roads). Liquids: water (for drinking and cooking) and palm oil (for preparing food).

ideas.t: Gives examples of solids
Gives examples of liquids
States a use

questions.q: Explain, with an example, how a material can change from one state to another.

parts.a: Heat or pressure can change a material from one state to another. For example, butter is a solid but it melts and becomes a liquid when it is heated. Cooking gas is stored as a liquid under pressure and turns into a gas when it is released.

ideas.t: Heat or pressure causes the change
Gives an example such as butter, ice or cooking gas
Says which state it changes from and to

questions.q: Kofi left an ice cube on a table in the hot sun for one hour. State the change that happened to the ice cube. Explain what caused this change.

parts.a: The ice cube melted. It changed from a solid to a liquid (water). The heat from the sun caused the change.

ideas.t: The ice cube melted into water (solid to liquid)
Heat from the sun caused it

pages.body: Liquids are important resources. Water is the most important liquid on earth. About sixty out of every hundred parts of your body is water. Your body needs water to digest food, control body temperature, move nutrients around in the blood and remove waste through urine and sweat. Other liquids also matter a lot. Cooking oil, fuel and blood all play big roles in our daily life, in industry, in transport and in health.

pages.title: Everyday uses of liquids
pages.body:
| **Liquid** | **Main uses** |
|---|---|
| Water | Drinking, cooking, washing, watering farms, making electricity from rivers |
| Cooking oil or palm oil | Preparing food, making soap, caring for skin |
| Petrol, kerosene or diesel | Fuel for cars, generators, lamps and stoves |
| Blood | Carries oxygen, nutrients and hormones around the body. It also removes waste |

questions.q: Which liquid is considered most essential for human survival?
questions.e: Understanding just how many different, essential purposes liquids serve helps explain why access to clean, reliable liquids, especially water, is considered such a basic human need.

questions.q: Water combined with soap is mainly important for
questions.e: Water combined with soap is essential for washing hands, bathing, cleaning clothes, and cleaning cooking utensils, all of which help prevent the spread of disease causing germs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a fuel liquid?
questions.e: Fuel liquids, such as petrol and kerosene, power vehicles, generators and lamps, while liquids such as water are also essential in agriculture for irrigating crops, and in many local industries, such as the gari processing and soa…

questions.q: Water is important in agriculture mainly for
questions.e: Fuel liquids, such as petrol and kerosene, power vehicles, generators and lamps, while liquids such as water are also essential in agriculture for irrigating crops, and in many local industries, such as the gari processing and soa…

questions.q: Cooking oil is important to human life mainly because it
o: Contributes to food preparation and nutrition
Has no nutritional value at all
questions.e: Cooking oil, palm wine, fruit juices, and soups are examples of liquids that contribute directly to human nutrition, either by providing energy and nutrients themselves or by being used to prepare other foods.

pages.title: Taking care of our liquids
pages.body:
Clean liquids, and clean water most of all, are limited. We must use them with care. Here are simple ways to take care of them.

1. Turn off taps when you are not using them and fix leaks quickly.
2. Store water and fuel in clean containers with covers and clear labels.
3. Do not pour waste, chemicals or rubbish into rivers, streams or wells.
4. Collect rain water and use it for jobs that do not need drinking water, such as watering plants.

> 🧪 **Activity 2** Work in a mixed group of three or four learners. List all the liquids used in your community in one day. Talk about this question. What would happen to your community if the main water source dried up for a month? Share your group's ideas and your ideas for taking care of water with the class.

questions.e: A person can survive for weeks without food, but only a few days without water, showing just how critical this particular liquid is to life.

questions.q: Preserving liquids for human use can include
questions.e: Preserving liquids can mean avoiding wasteful use, such as leaving a tap running unnecessarily, protecting water sources such as rivers and boreholes from pollution, and storing liquids such as drinking water safely and hygienical…

questions.e: Many communities in Ghana face challenges accessing enough clean water, particularly during the dry season, which is one reason government and community organisations invest in boreholes, water storage tanks, and public education …

questions.q: Why should we take care of the water in our community? Give two reasons.

parts.a: Clean water is limited, so we must use it with care. Our bodies need water to digest food, control temperature and remove waste, and we also use water for cooking, washing and watering farms. If it is wasted or polluted there may not be enough for everyone.

ideas.t: Clean water is limited and can run out
We need water to live and stay healthy

questions.q: A market woman wants to keep her palm oil fresh and stop it from spilling while she carries it to market. Using what you know about liquids, suggest two things she should do.

parts.a: She should store the palm oil in a clean container and cover it tightly so it does not spill or get dirty. She can also label the container clearly.

ideas.t: Use a clean container
Cover it with a tight lid so it does not spill

pages.body:
Solids matter just as much as liquids. They give us the raw materials for shelter, tools, furniture and roads. Many solids, such as food crops, salt and minerals, are also needed for good nutrition and for industry.

## Everyday uses of solids

| **Solid** | **Main uses** |
|---|---|
| Wood | Building, furniture, firewood, making charcoal |
| Stone, rock or laterite | Foundations for buildings, roads, gravel |
| Iron and other metals | Tools, nails, roofing sheets, vehicles, machines |
| Clay | Pottery, bricks, ceramics |
| Salt | Keeping food fresh, adding taste to food, industry |

Many useful solids, such as timber and minerals, take a very long time to form. Some cannot be replaced at all. So we must use them wisely. We should plant new trees to replace the ones we cut down. We should also stop illegal or careless mining, often called galamsey, because it destroys land and water bodies.

> 🧪 **Activity 3** Name five solid materials in your surroundings that help humans to survive. In your notebook, draw or describe one useful object you could make from a local solid material. Explain its use.

questions.q: Soil is essential to life mainly because it
o: Has no connection to plant growth
Is used only for building roads
Supports plant growth by supplying water and nutrients
questions.e: Soil is a solid material that supports nearly all plant growth, since plants root themselves in soil and draw water and nutrients from it, and since humans and animals ultimately depend on plants, directly or indirectly, for food.

questions.q: Wood is valued as a solid mainly for its
o: Inability to be shaped at all
questions.e: Wood's particular combination of strength, workability and availability has made it one of the most widely used solid materials throughout human history.

questions.q: Rocks and stones are commonly used for
questions.e: Rocks and stones are solid materials used for building foundations, walls, and roads, valued for their hardness and durability.

questions.q: Limestone, a type of rock, is a key raw material in
questions.e: Some rocks are also processed into other useful materials, such as limestone, which, as studied in an earlier lesson on industry, is a key raw material in cement production.

questions.q: Metals such as iron are valued mainly for their
o: Strength and ability to be shaped into tools
questions.e: Metals such as iron are solid materials extracted from ores found in the ground, valued for their strength and ability to be shaped into tools, nails, and construction materials, as studied in relation to agricultural tools elsewh…

questions.q: Overusing solid resources, such as clearing forests too quickly, can lead to
questions.e: Overusing or poorly managing solid resources, such as clearing forests faster than they can regrow, or allowing soil to erode and lose its fertility, can permanently reduce how much of these valuable solids remain available, affec…

questions.q: Preserving useful solid materials mainly means
o: Ensuring resources remain available for the future
Using resources as wastefully as possible
questions.e: Since useful solid resources such as fertile soil, forests, and mineral deposits are not unlimited, preserving them carefully is essential for ensuring they remain available to support life in the future.

questions.q: Soil erosion can be reduced through
o: Terracing and other soil conservation techniques
questions.e: Many communities practise sustainable solid resource management, such as planting new trees to replace those harvested for wood, or using terracing and other soil conservation techniques to prevent erosion on farmland, showing tha…

questions.q: Modelling an object from solid materials mainly helps to
o: Build practical understanding of how solids meet human needs
Remove the need for further study
questions.e: Creating a simple model of a useful object from solid materials, such as a small clay pot, a wooden toy, or a stone marker, using materials available in your environment, helps build practical understanding of how solids can be sh…

questions.q: Planting new trees to replace harvested wood is an example of
questions.e: Many communities practise sustainable solid resource management, such as planting new trees to replace those harvested for wood, or using terracing and other soil conservation techniques to prevent erosion on farmland, showing tha…

questions.q: A builder wants to make a small tank to store rain water for the dry season. Suggest one solid material he could use to build the tank. Explain why this material is suitable.

parts.a: He could use stone (or iron, or bricks made from clay). Solids have a fixed shape and volume and are strong, so the tank will keep its shape and hold the water.

ideas.t: Suggests a solid material
Gives a reason such as strong or keeps its shape

pages.title: Taking care of our solids
pages.body: Useful solid materials such as metals, timber, stone, sand, clay and plastics do not last for ever, and many cannot be replaced once they are used up. Gold, bauxite and manganese are mined in Ghana, and a mineral that has been dug out does not grow back. Trees take many years to replace. We therefore need to preserve useful solids so that people in the future can also use them.

pages.title: Ways of preserving solids
pages.body:
- Reuse solid items such as bottles, containers and bags and do not throw them away after one use.
- Recycle metals, glass, paper and plastics so that less new material has to be mined or made.
- Plant a tree for every tree that is cut and avoid bush burning.
- Protect iron and steel from rusting by painting, oiling or keeping them dry.
- Store tools, books and furniture properly so that they last longer.
- Mine sand, stone and minerals only in approved places, because illegal mining destroys land and rivers.

questions.q: Give three ways of preserving useful solid materials

parts.a: Any three of: reuse solid items such as bottles, containers and bags; recycle metals, glass, paper and plastics; plant a tree for every tree that is cut and avoid bush burning; protect iron and steel from rusting by painting, oiling or keeping them dry; store tools, books and furniture properly; mine sand, stone and minerals only in approved places.

ideas.t: Reuse solid items
Recycle metals, glass, paper or plastics
Plant trees and avoid bush burning
Protect iron and steel from rusting
Store tools, books and furniture properly
Mine only in approved places

questions.q: Why should minerals such as gold and bauxite be used carefully

parts.a: A mineral that has been mined does not grow back, so it cannot be replaced once it is used up. People in the future also need these materials.

ideas.t: A mineral that has been mined does not grow back
It cannot be replaced once it is used up, so future people need it

pages.title: What is the periodic table
pages.body:
All matter is built from basic building blocks called elements. An element is a pure substance. It cannot be broken down into a simpler substance by ordinary chemical means. Scientists have arranged all the known elements into a chart called the periodic table. The elements are placed in order of their atomic number. The atomic number tells us how many protons are inside one atom of the element. Elements standing in the same column of the table are called a group. Elements in the same group behave in a similar way.

[[img:igccbrie1]]

pages.title: Three big families of elements
pages.body:
| **Family** | **Key properties** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Metals | Shiny. Good at carrying heat and electricity. Can be hammered into sheets. Can be drawn into wire. Solid at room temperature, except mercury | Iron (Fe), Sodium (Na), Copper (Cu), Aluminium (Al) |
| Nonmetals | Dull look. Poor at carrying heat and electricity, except graphite. Brittle if solid. Can be solid, liquid or gas at room temperature | Carbon (C), Oxygen (O), Nitrogen (N), Sulphur (S) |
| Noble gases | Colourless gases with no smell. They almost never react with other elements. Found in the last column of the table | Helium (He), Neon (Ne), Argon (Ar) |

questions.q: The periodic table is best described as
o: A random list of elements with no pattern
A table listing elements in a random alphabetical order only
An organised chart arranging elements by pattern and property
questions.e: The periodic table is an organised chart listing every known chemical element, arranged in a specific, carefully designed order that groups elements with similar properties near one another.

questions.q: Metals are generally
o: Poor conductors of heat and electricity
Shiny and good conductors of heat and electricity
questions.e: Metals are elements that are generally shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and can be hammered or drawn into shapes without breaking.

questions.q: Elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of their
questions.e: Every element in the periodic table is arranged in order of its atomic number, a number that represents how many protons are found in the nucleus of that element's atoms, starting from hydrogen, with atomic number 1, and increasin…

questions.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table generally
o: Have no properties in common at all
questions.e: Elements arranged in the same vertical column of the periodic table, called a group, share similar chemical properties, since they tend to have a similar arrangement of the outermost electrons in their atoms.

questions.q: Name the three big families of elements in the periodic table. Give one property of each family.

parts.a: The three families are metals, nonmetals and noble gases. Metals are shiny and good at carrying heat and electricity. Nonmetals look dull and carry heat and electricity poorly. Noble gases are colourless gases that almost never react with other elements.

ideas.t: Metals, with a property such as shiny or good conductors
Nonmetals, with a property such as dull or brittle
Noble gases, with a property such as not reacting

pages.title: The first twenty elements
pages.body:
You should be able to name and write the correct symbol for the first twenty elements, in order of atomic number.

| **No.** | **Element** | **Symbol** | **No.** | **Element** | **Symbol** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hydrogen | H | 11 | Sodium | Na |
| 2 | Helium | He | 12 | Magnesium | Mg |
| 3 | Lithium | Li | 13 | Aluminium | Al |
| 4 | Beryllium | Be | 14 | Silicon | Si |
| 5 | Boron | B | 15 | Phosphorus | P |
| 6 | Carbon | C | 16 | Sulphur | S |
| 7 | Nitrogen | N | 17 | Chlorine | Cl |
| 8 | Oxygen | O | 18 | Argon | Ar |
| 9 | Fluorine | F | 19 | Potassium | K |
| 10 | Neon | Ne | 20 | Calcium | Ca |

Blue cells are metals. Green cells are nonmetals. Peach cells are noble gases. Look at the pattern. The elements are placed in order, from left to right and from top to bottom, by atomic number. Elements in the same column, such as Lithium, Sodium and Potassium, behave alike. This is because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

[[img:i67mp36q2]]

> 🧪 **Activity 4** Draw a simple grid of the first twenty elements in order. Write each element's name and symbol. Circle the metals in one colour. Circle the nonmetals in a second colour. Circle the noble gases in a third colour. Work with a partner. Explain to each other why elements in the same column of the periodic table behave alike.

questions.q: An element's chemical symbol is
o: A long, full sentence describing the element
A short abbreviation, usually one or two letters
questions.e: An element is a pure substance made of only one type of atom, and each element is represented by a chemical symbol, a short abbreviation usually made of one or two letters.

questions.q: Which of the following is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
questions.e: An element is a pure substance made of only one type of atom, and each element is represented by a chemical symbol, a short abbreviation usually made of one or two letters.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a metal among the first 20 elements?
questions.e: Lithium, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, potassium and calcium are examples of metals found among the first 20 elements, and metals make up the majority of known elements overall.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a nonmetal among the first 20 elements?
questions.e: Hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and chlorine are examples of nonmetals found among the first 20 elements, and nonmetals are essential to life, forming the basis of the air we breathe and the molecules that make up living thing…

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a noble gas among the first 20 elements?
questions.e: Helium, neon and argon are examples of noble gases found among the first 20 elements, and helium is well known for its use in filling balloons, since it is much less dense than air.

questions.q: Noble gases are best described as
questions.e: Noble gases are a special group of elements that are extremely unreactive, rarely combining with other elements under normal conditions, which is why they are described as 'noble', existing largely independently rather than readil…

questions.q: Write the correct symbol for these elements. Sodium. Oxygen. Carbon. Potassium.

parts.a: Sodium is Na. Oxygen is O. Carbon is C. Potassium is K.

ideas.t: Sodium is Na
Oxygen is O
Carbon is C
Potassium is K

questions.q: Look at these elements. Sodium, Chlorine, Neon. Sort each one into its correct family, metal, nonmetal or noble gas. Give one reason for each answer.

parts.a: Sodium is a metal because it is shiny and carries heat and electricity well. Chlorine is a nonmetal. Neon is a noble gas because it almost never reacts with other elements.

ideas.t: Sodium is a metal
Chlorine is a nonmetal
Neon is a noble gas
Gives a reason such as shiny, conducts, dull or does not react

pages.body:
- Matter has three common states. They are solid, liquid and gas. They differ in how their particles are packed and how the particles move.
- A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. A liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
- The state of a material can change with heat and pressure. Cooking gas and melted butter are good examples.
- Liquids such as water and oil, and solids such as wood, metal and stone, are important resources. We must use and care for them well.
- All matter is made of elements. The elements are arranged in the periodic table by atomic number.
- Elements fall into three big families. They are metals, nonmetals and noble gases. Each family has its own properties.
- Elements in the same column of the periodic table, called a group, share similar properties.
- A change of state such as melting, freezing, boiling, evaporation, condensation or sublimation happens when a substance takes in or gives out heat energy.
- Useful solids such as metals, timber and minerals must be preserved by reusing, recycling, replanting trees and preventing rust, because many of them cannot be replaced.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Matter | Anything that has mass and takes up space |
| State of matter | The form matter is in. It can be solid, liquid or gas |
| Solid | A state of matter with a fixed shape and fixed volume. The particles only shake in place |
| Liquid | A state of matter with a fixed volume but no fixed shape. The particles can slide past each other |
| Gas | A state of matter with no fixed shape and no fixed volume. The particles move freely and fast |
| Squeeze test (compressibility) | How easily a material can be pressed into a smaller space |
| Taking care of resources (conservation) | Using and protecting resources so they are not wasted or spoiled |
| Element | A pure substance made of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into a simpler substance |
| Atomic number | The number of protons in the middle of one atom. It tells us the order of elements in the periodic table |
| Periodic table | A chart that arranges all known elements in order of atomic number. Elements with similar properties are grouped together |
| Metal | An element that is usually shiny and bendable. It carries heat and electricity well |
| Nonmetal | An element that is usually dull and breaks easily if solid. It carries heat and electricity poorly |
| Noble gas | A gas element that almost never reacts with other elements |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The three states of matter: changes of state

pages.body:
| **Change of state** | **What happens** | **Heat energy** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Melting** | A solid changes to a liquid | Heat is taken in | Ice melts into water and butter melts in a hot pan |
| **Freezing** | A liquid changes to a solid | Heat is given out | Water freezes into ice in a freezer |
| **Boiling** | A liquid changes to a gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature | Heat is taken in | Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius to form steam |
| **Evaporation** | A liquid changes to a gas at its surface at any temperature | Heat is taken in | Wet clothes dry on a line |
| **Condensation** | A gas changes to a liquid | Heat is given out | Drops of water form on the outside of a cold bottle |
| **Sublimation** | A solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid | Heat is taken in | Naphthalene balls slowly become smaller |

Under normal air pressure, pure ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius and pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. These fixed temperatures are called the melting point and the boiling point.

> 🧪 **Activity 1** Work in a group. Collect eight to ten materials from your school compound or home. Examples are a stone, water, cooking oil, air in a balloon, chalk, an exercise book, palm wine and a nail. Draw a table with these headings. Material, Texture, Appearance, Colour, Shape, State. Fill in the table for each material. Talk about your answers as a class. Explain why you placed each material under its state.

questions.q: Name the change of state that takes place when ice becomes water

parts.a: Ice becoming water is melting, and water vapour becoming water is condensation.

ideas.t: Melting
Condensation

questions.q: State the difference between boiling and evaporation

parts.a: Boiling changes a liquid to a gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature (100 degrees Celsius for water). Evaporation changes a liquid to a gas at its surface at any temperature.

ideas.t: Boiling: throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature
Evaporation: at the surface at any temperature

questions.q: What is sublimation

parts.a: Sublimation is when a solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid. For example, naphthalene balls slowly become smaller.

ideas.t: A solid changes directly to a gas
An example such as naphthalene balls

questions.q: Drops of water form on the outside of a bottle

parts.a: The change of state is condensation. Water vapour in the air touches the cold bottle, cools and changes to liquid water, so the water comes from the air.

ideas.t: Condensation
The water vapour in the air
Cools or touches the cold bottle

questions.q: Name three ways a solid is different from a gas.

parts.a: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume, so it fills all the space in its container. The particles of a solid are packed close together and only vibrate, but the particles of a gas are far apart and move fast in every direction. A gas can be squeezed easily, a solid cannot.

ideas.t: A solid has a fixed shape, a gas does not
A solid has a fixed volume, a gas fills its container
Particles in a solid are packed close, in a gas they are far apart
Particles in a solid only vibrate, in a gas they move fast and freely
A gas can be squeezed (compressed), a solid cannot

questions.q: Give two examples of solids and two examples of liquids from your community. State one use of each.

parts.a: Solids: wood (for building and furniture) and stone (for foundations and roads). Liquids: water (for drinking and cooking) and palm oil (for preparing food).

ideas.t: Gives examples of solids
Gives examples of liquids
States a use

questions.q: Explain, with an example, how a material can change from one state to another.

parts.a: Heat or pressure can change a material from one state to another. For example, butter is a solid but it melts and becomes a liquid when it is heated. Cooking gas is stored as a liquid under pressure and turns into a gas when it is released.

ideas.t: Heat or pressure causes the change
Gives an example such as butter, ice or cooking gas
Says which state it changes from and to

questions.q: Why should we take care of the water in our community? Give two reasons.

parts.a: Clean water is limited, so we must use it with care. Our bodies need water to digest food, control temperature and remove waste, and we also use water for cooking, washing and watering farms. If it is wasted or polluted there may not be enough for everyone.

ideas.t: Clean water is limited and can run out
We need water to live and stay healthy
Water is used for cooking, washing and farming
Water can be wasted or polluted

questions.q: Write the correct symbol for these elements. Sodium. Oxygen. Carbon. Potassium.

parts.a: Sodium is Na. Oxygen is O. Carbon is C. Potassium is K.

ideas.t: Sodium is Na
Oxygen is O
Carbon is C
Potassium is K

questions.q: Name the three big families of elements in the periodic table. Give one property of each family.

parts.a: The three families are metals, nonmetals and noble gases. Metals are shiny and good at carrying heat and electricity. Nonmetals look dull and carry heat and electricity poorly. Noble gases are colourless gases that almost never react with other elements.

ideas.t: Metals, with a property such as shiny or good conductors
Nonmetals, with a property such as dull or brittle
Noble gases, with a property such as not reacting

questions.q: A market woman wants to keep her palm oil fresh and stop it from spilling while she carries it to market. Using what you know about liquids, suggest two things she should do.

parts.a: She should store the palm oil in a clean container and cover it tightly so it does not spill or get dirty. She can also label the container clearly.

ideas.t: Use a clean container
Cover it with a tight lid so it does not spill
Label the container

questions.q: Kofi left an ice cube on a table in the hot sun for one hour. State the change that happened to the ice cube. Explain what caused this change.

parts.a: The ice cube melted. It changed from a solid to a liquid (water). The heat from the sun caused the change.

ideas.t: The ice cube melted into water (solid to liquid)
Heat from the sun caused it

questions.q: Look at these elements. Sodium, Chlorine, Neon. Sort each one into its correct family, metal, nonmetal or noble gas. Give one reason for each answer.

parts.a: Sodium is a metal because it is shiny and carries heat and electricity well. Chlorine is a nonmetal. Neon is a noble gas because it almost never reacts with other elements.

ideas.t: Sodium is a metal
Chlorine is a nonmetal
Neon is a noble gas
Gives a reason such as shiny, conducts, dull or does not react

questions.q: Cooking gas in your home is stored inside a strong metal cylinder with a tight cover. Explain why it cannot be stored in an open plastic bag instead.

parts.a: Cooking gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume, so it would spread out and escape from an open plastic bag. It is stored as a liquid under pressure, so it needs a strong metal cylinder with a tight cover.

ideas.t: A gas spreads out and would escape from an open bag
The cylinder is strong and tight to hold the gas under pressure

questions.q: A builder wants to make a small tank to store rain water for the dry season. Suggest one solid material he could use to build the tank. Explain why this material is suitable.

parts.a: He could use stone (or iron, or bricks made from clay). Solids have a fixed shape and volume and are strong, so the tank will keep its shape and hold the water.

ideas.t: Suggests a solid material
Gives a reason such as strong or keeps its shape

questions.q: Think about your community. Choose one liquid resource and one solid resource that people may be wasting or misusing.

parts.q: Name the liquid resource and the solid resource you have chosen.
parts.a: Liquid resource: water. Solid resource: trees (timber) or minerals.

ideas.t: Names a liquid resource
Names a solid resource

parts.q: For each resource, explain how it is being used or misused.
parts.a: Water is wasted when taps are left running or when rubbish is thrown into rivers. Trees are cut down without planting new ones, and careless or illegal mining (galamsey) destroys land.

ideas.t: Says how the liquid is used or misused
Says how the solid is used or misused

parts.q: Describe one effect this misuse could have on your community.
parts.a: Rivers and wells may become dirty or dry up, so there may not be enough clean water. Destroyed land and water bodies harm farming and the health of people in the community.

ideas.t: Describes a harmful effect
Says who or what is affected

parts.q: Suggest two steps people in your community can take to look after each resource better.
parts.a: Turn off taps and fix leaks. Store water in clean covered containers. Do not pour waste or rubbish into rivers, streams or wells. Collect rain water for watering plants. Plant new trees to replace those cut down and stop illegal mining (galamsey).

ideas.t: Turn off taps and fix leaks
Store water in clean, covered containers
Do not pour waste or rubbish into rivers or wells
Collect rain water
Plant new trees to replace those cut down
Stop illegal mining (galamsey)
Use resources wisely and with care

questions.q: Name the change of state that takes place when ice becomes water

parts.a: Ice becoming water is melting, and water vapour becoming water is condensation.

ideas.t: Melting
Condensation

questions.q: State the difference between boiling and evaporation

parts.a: Boiling changes a liquid to a gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature (100 degrees Celsius for water). Evaporation changes a liquid to a gas at its surface at any temperature.

ideas.t: Boiling: throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature
Evaporation: at the surface at any temperature

questions.q: What is sublimation

parts.a: Sublimation is when a solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid. For example, naphthalene balls slowly become smaller.

ideas.t: A solid changes directly to a gas
An example such as naphthalene balls

questions.q: Drops of water form on the outside of a bottle

parts.a: The change of state is condensation. Water vapour in the air touches the cold bottle, cools and changes to liquid water, so the water comes from the air.

ideas.t: Condensation
The water vapour in the air
Cools or touches the cold bottle

questions.q: Give three ways of preserving useful solid materials

parts.a: Any three of: reuse solid items such as bottles, containers and bags; recycle metals, glass, paper and plastics; plant a tree for every tree that is cut and avoid bush burning; protect iron and steel from rusting by painting, oiling or keeping them dry; store tools, books and furniture properly; mine sand, stone and minerals only in approved places.

ideas.t: Reuse solid items
Recycle metals, glass, paper or plastics
Plant trees and avoid bush burning
Protect iron and steel from rusting
Store tools, books and furniture properly
Mine only in approved places

questions.q: Why should minerals such as gold and bauxite be used carefully

parts.a: A mineral that has been mined does not grow back, so it cannot be replaced once it is used up. People in the future also need these materials.

ideas.t: A mineral that has been mined does not grow back
It cannot be replaced once it is used up, so future people need it
